**My answer: impossible—though I regard this as a defensible philosophical commitment, not an established theorem about reality.**

By a true contradiction, I mean that a proposition and its negation are both true, with meanings, time, and relevant respects held fixed. Conflicting descriptions, inconsistent databases, and objects changing over time do not qualify.

My main reason is that negation seems to express precisely the exclusion of what it negates. If “not P” can be true alongside P, I need an account of what makes it *negation*, rather than some weaker relation such as opposition or incompatibility under normal conditions. Dialetheists have sophisticated answers, but I do not think those answers are more compelling than preserving exclusion and revising other assumptions.

The strongest pressure comes from semantic paradoxes, especially the liar sentence: “This sentence is not true.” Here I favor restricting the principles governing truth and self-reference rather than accepting a true contradiction. That choice has costs—particularly the loss of an unrestricted, fully transparent truth predicate. But the paradox establishes that some attractive commitments cannot all survive; it does not uniquely identify noncontradiction as the commitment to abandon.

Importantly, **paraconsistent reasoning can be useful even if true contradictions are impossible**. We need ways to reason from inconsistent evidence without concluding everything. Tolerating contradictions in our information is not the same as finding them in reality.

My uncertainty is greatest about semantic paradoxes. I see genuine theoretical competition there, not a decisive refutation of dialetheism.

text:
I defend the classical view: **true contradictions are impossible**, not merely non-actual.  

My reason is metaphysical rather than just logical. Truth, as I understand it, requires a truthmaker—something about the world that makes a claim true. For “P and not-P” to be true, reality would have to include a single state of affairs that both obtains and fails to obtain in the same respect. I do not think that is a coherent possibility. It is not that the world happens not to contain such facts; rather, “contradictory fact” is a defective specification of fact.

Apparent true contradictions—liar sentences, boundary cases, inconsistent laws, quantum puzzles—are better explained as semantic pathology, vagueness, incomplete models, or inconsistent *information*, not inconsistent reality. Paraconsistent logics are valuable for reasoning with inconsistent data or beliefs, but I treat them as tools for modeling thought, not as evidence that reality itself is inconsistent.

Where I am uncertain: I am less confident about whether this impossibility should be called logical or metaphysical. Paraconsistent logicians can block explosion, so one cannot simply assume classical logic settles it. My claim is stronger and more vulnerable: there is no truthmaker for a contradiction. If someone showed a concrete, non-reinterpretable case of a single fact both obtaining and not obtaining, I would have to revise my view. I currently see no such case.

# Impossible, though with only moderate confidence (roughly 70%)

**First, the middle option is unstable.** If the law of non-contradiction holds at all, it holds as a logical law, and logical laws don't hold contingently. If LNC can fail somewhere in logical space, it is hard to see what would make the actual world a privileged exception. "Possible but non-actual" makes sense only for impossible-worlds semantics, where "possible" has been redefined. So the real contest is between *impossible* and *actual*.

**Why not actual?** The strongest case for dialetheism is the Liar ("this sentence is not true"), combined with the attractive principle that "*p*" is true iff *p*. Priest's move is to accept naive truth and let the Liar be both true and false. But this has a cost I think is worse than its rivals' costs: it undermines *exclusion*. If something can be both true and false, then asserting "*p* is false" no longer rules out *p*. Priest's attempts to recover rejection, or "just false," either rebuild the paradox in a new form or treat rejection as a primitive speech act. That act then has no content-level guarantee, leaving the theory unable to say what it denies.

**The rival costs are more contained.** Approaches like Kripke's fixed points, contextualism, or restricting the truth schema each limit the truth predicate in some way. That is real damage, but it is confined to semantic vocabulary. The dialetheist's damage spreads to disagreement itself.

**Other proposed dialetheias are weaker.** Cases from motion, vagueness, legal conflicts, and borderline predicates all have good consistent treatments, such as supervaluation, indeterminacy, or ambiguity resolution. Nothing empirical has ever forced a contradiction on us.

**Where I'm uncertain:** Every theory of the semantic paradoxes faces revenge problems, including mine. The consistent theorist cannot fully express their own truth theory in their own language. If that limit is judged as bad as the dialetheist's trouble with exclusion, the scales come closer to even than I've suggested. I don't think they balance, but I don't regard dialetheism as confused. It is a serious position paying a price I judge too high.

label: Grok
text: True contradictions are impossible. A proposition and its negation cannot both be true, because the law of non-contradiction is a condition on the very idea of truth and assertion, not an optional axiom we might drop when paradoxes get awkward. If “P and not-P” could hold, the difference between accepting and rejecting a claim would collapse, and with it any stable notion of evidence, entailment, or disagreement. Paraconsistent systems show that one can block explosion formally and still do mathematics; they do not show that any such contradiction is true of anything. The liar sentence and its kin are better read as cases where language fails to express a proposition, or where our semantic theory needs restriction, than as revelations that reality contains truths that are also false. I am unsure which precise diagnosis of the paradoxes will win, but the cost of dialetheism—undermining the contrast that makes inquiry possible—is higher than the alternatives. “Possible but non-actual” fares no better: if a contradiction is not even logically possible, it cannot be a non-actual possibility either.

label: Gemini
text:
True contradictions are **impossible**. Reality cannot simultaneously instantiate a state of affairs and its exact negation. 

The strongest case for *actual* contradictions—dialetheism—relies on semantic and set-theoretic paradoxes, chiefly the Liar ("This sentence is false"). Dialetheists argue that taking our semantic rules at face value forces us to accept the Liar as both true and false. I reject this because it mistakes a glitch in our representational machinery for a feature of reality. Natural language evolved for practical coordination, not formal consistency. Our everyday concept of "truth" is governed by naive, over-permissive rules. When self-reference exploits those rules, the sentence fails to express a coherent proposition; it yields a truth-value gap or semantic malfunction, not a true contradiction.

Empirical candidates fare even worse. Quantum superposition is routinely mischaracterized in popularizations as a particle being "both here and not here." In fact, the system occupies a single, mathematically consistent state vector; a contradiction only appears if we force ill-fitting classical predicates onto quantum phenomena. Similarly, borderline cases of vagueness—calling a dusk sky "both dark and not dark"—reflect imprecise linguistic boundaries, not contradictory facts.

Why *impossible* rather than *possible but non-actual*? Because negation is defined by exclusion. A putative possible world containing both $P$ and $\neg P$ isn't a world where a contradiction holds; it is a scenario where the symbol "$\neg$" has quietly stopped meaning negation.

Where I remain genuinely uncertain is how to resolve semantic "revenge" paradoxes (such as "This sentence is either false or semantically defective"). Every classical attempt to banish contradictions via truth-value gaps or Tarskian hierarchies eventually hits severe expressive limitations. I do not know if a unified, paradox-free theory of truth is achievable. Still, our inability to build a flawless linguistic mirror does not mean reality itself is cracked.
